anchor: Daughter of the Voice of God
title: 'Stern Daughter of the Voice of God'
greek: Hebrew bat qôl, 'daughter of the voice'
short: Duty is the offspring of God's commandment, a phrase recalling Milton's Eve and the rabbinic 'daughter of the voice'.
body: In Paradise Lost IX.652-653 Eve says that God left his command 'Sole Daughter of his voice': the prohibition is the child of the divine word. Wordsworth personifies Duty in the same way. The phrase also corresponds to the rabbinic bat qôl, literally 'daughter of the voice', the heavenly voice that conveyed God's will after prophecy ceased. The opening 'Stern' and the ode's apostrophic form also follow Gray's 'Hymn to Adversity', which begins 'Daughter of Jove, relentless Power'.

sources.cite: Milton, Paradise Lost IX.651-654 (Dartmouth Milton Reading Room)
'Bat Kol', Jewish Encyclopedia (1906)
Thomas Gray, 'Hymn to Adversity' (1753), Thomas Gray Archive

title: date, model and purpose
short: Begun by spring 1804 and published in Poems, in Two Volumes (1807); modelled, as Wordsworth said, on Gray's ode to Adversity.
body: An early form of the poem, lacking the title and first stanza, was finished before April 1804, so it predates the death at sea of the poet's brother John in February 1805; a link between the two is therefore chronologically impossible for that early version. The Fenwick note says that the ode 'is on the model of Gray's Ode to Adversity, which is copied from Horace's Ode to Fortune' (Odes I.35), and admits that his wife and sister often teased him for forgetting this 'dedication of myself to the stern law-giver'. The poem marks a turn from the faith in spontaneous impulse of 1798. In 1837 Wordsworth added a Latin motto from Seneca (Epistles 120), not printed here, praising a man good by habit who cannot act except rightly.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem
Thomas Gray, 'Hymn to Adversity' (1753), Thomas Gray Archive
Horace, Odes I.35 (Perseus)

anchor: a Light to guide, a Rod
title: Light and Rod
short: Duty both guides (a light) and corrects (a rod), the two functions of God's law in the Psalms and Proverbs.
body: 'Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path' (Psalm 119:105); 'thy rod and thy staff they comfort me' (Psalm 23:4); and the rod of correction in Proverbs 13:24 and 22:15. Duty is 'victory and law' when 'empty terrors overawe', that is, it gives firmness against groundless fears. The stanza ends in a line of six stresses, an alexandrine ('a glorious ministry'), the closing feature of every stanza, which slows and solemnizes the end.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Psalm 119:105
The Bible (KJV), Psalm 23:4
The Bible (KJV), Proverbs 13:24

title: stanza form
short: Eight-line stanzas rhyming ababccdd: seven tetrameters closed by an alexandrine.
body: Gray's 'Hymn to Adversity' used an eight-line stanza closed by a longer line; Wordsworth adapts it with a hexameter close, a feature also found in the Spenserian stanza. The weighty final line recurs as a moral summation in each stanza ('teach them to stand fast!', 'according to their need'). The 1807 text of the first stanza ended 'And calm'st the weary strife of frail humanity!'; the reading here ('From strife and from despair; a glorious ministry') is a later revision.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem
Thomas Gray, 'Hymn to Adversity' (1753), Thomas Gray Archive

title: genial
short: Pertaining to one's innate nature or 'genius'; here the instinctive, happy goodness of youth that needs no rule.
body: 'Genial' in this older sense means belonging to one's natural disposition, productive and life-giving (OED), not merely friendly. Wordsworth's 'Tintern Abbey' speaks of 'my genial spirits', and Coleridge's 'Dejection: An Ode' (1802) laments 'My genial spirits fail'. The second stanza describes those who do good by instinct, 'Who do thy work, and know it not', and blesses them; but the poet asks Duty to support them if they 'totter'. In 1807 this stanza closed differently, with a prayer that if they fail Duty's 'saving arms' be cast around them; the ending here is a later revision.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'genial, adj.'
William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem

title: 'Who do thy work, and know it not'
short: Those who are spontaneously good serve Duty without being aware of it.
body: The line captures the poem's starting position: the ideal of 1798, that a heart in harmony with nature does right without rules. The poem does not reject that ideal but questions whether it is reliable; the speaker counts himself among those who trusted it 'Too blindly'.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem

title: 'When love is an unerring light'
short: A future state when love itself will guide without error, and joy will be its own security.
body: The stanza looks forward to a condition where duty and desire coincide. The idea recalls Augustine's precept 'love, and do what you will' (dilige, et quod vis fac, Homilies on the First Epistle of John 7.8): perfected love needs no external law. Those who 'in the main' (for the most part) live by this faith are 'bless'd', yet even they need 'that other strength' of duty when love falters. 'Even now' implies that this state belongs fully only to an ideal future.

sources.cite: Augustine, In epistulam Ioannis ad Parthos tractatus 7.8
William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem

title: the poet's confession
short: The fourth stanza turns to the speaker's own life: untested, guided only by himself, he has put off unwelcome tasks.
body: 'Untried' means not yet tested by hardship. 'No sport of every random gust' insists that he was not merely unstable, but he has 'Too blindly' trusted his own guidance. The confession matches the Fenwick note, where Wordsworth admits he has often been a 'transgressor'.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem

title: 'Me this uncharter'd freedom tires'
short: Freedom without any charter or rule, wearying in its very lack of limits.
body: A charter grants specified rights or privileges; 'unchartered' freedom is liberty without definition or bounds. Blake's 'London' (1794) had used 'charter'd' bitterly of streets and river, owned and regulated. Wordsworth's paradox, that boundless liberty is a burden, anticipates his sonnet 'Nuns fret not at their convent's narrow room' (written 1802, published 1807), where the sonnet's 'scanty plot of ground' is a relief from 'too much liberty'. Some readers see a political as well as a personal retreat here, from revolutionary freedom to order.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem
William Blake, 'London', Songs of Experience (1794)
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'chartered, adj.'

title: 'My hopes no more must change their name'
short: His hopes should no longer keep shifting into fears or new desires; he longs for a 'repose which ever is the same'.
body: The line is compressed. Most readers take it to mean that hopes subject to 'chance desires' constantly turn into something else, disappointment, fear or a new wish, and so 'change their name'. The longing for unchanging repose answers this restlessness. The paradox is that the repose sought is not inactivity but stable obedience. Critics have found in the stanza a candid portrait of the strain of living by impulse.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem
E. de Selincourt and Helen Darbishire, eds., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth (Oxford, 1940-49), notes to the poem

anchor: Yet not the less would I
title: the suppressed stanza
short: A stanza in the 1807 printing that Wordsworth later dropped from his collected editions.
body: The 1807 first edition included this stanza; Wordsworth later omitted it. It qualifies the submission of the poem: the speaker will still act according to his 'own wish' and wants to feel that his 'submissiveness was choice'. He values denial and restraint only as far as they 'breed a second Will more wise', a self chosen rather than imposed. The quotation 'precepts over dignified' is presented as a citation but its source has not been securely identified; it mocks pompous moralizing ('the school of pride'). Its removal makes the later poem more simply devotional.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem
E. de Selincourt and Helen Darbishire, eds., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth (Oxford, 1940-49), notes to the poem

title: 'Stern Lawgiver!' and Duty's smile
short: Duty, though stern, wears 'the Godhead's most benignant grace': the lawgiver is also beautiful and kind.
body: 'Lawgiver' recalls Moses and the law of Sinai, and the epithet 'Stern' recalls Gray's 'Stern rugged Nurse' in the 'Hymn to Adversity', where the goddess is asked to wear a gentler form. The shift from severity to grace is the turn of the ode: Duty's smile is the fairest thing known. 'Benignant' means kindly, gracious. The poem here moves from moral psychology to a cosmic vision.

sources.cite: Thomas Gray, 'Hymn to Adversity' (1753), Thomas Gray Archive
William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem

title: 'Flowers laugh before thee'
short: Nature rejoices in Duty's presence; fragrance follows her steps.
body: Nature rejoices in Duty's presence and fragrance follows her steps. Classical poetry gives similar attributes to goddesses of love: in Hesiod's Theogony (194ff.) grass springs up beneath Aphrodite's feet. The biblical image of the hills breaking into singing and the trees clapping their hands (Isaiah 55:12) is also close. Wordsworth transfers to Duty attributes traditionally given to love and beauty, uniting the moral law with natural joy.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem
The Bible (KJV), Isaiah 55:12

title: Duty and the stars
short: The same law that rules the conscience keeps the stars in their courses: moral and natural order are one.
body: The ancient heavens are 'fresh and strong' through Duty: the order of the universe is itself a kind of obedience. Readers often compare Kant's conclusion to the Critique of Practical Reason (1788), which joins 'the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me' as twin objects of awe; Wordsworth probably knew Kant's ideas, if at all, through Coleridge, so the parallel is one of thought rather than a direct source. The idea also has biblical roots in Psalm 19, where the heavens declaring God's glory are followed by praise of his law.

sources.cite: Kant, Critique of Practical Reason (1788), Conclusion
The Bible (KJV), Psalm 19:1-8
William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem

title: awful
short: Awe-inspiring, worthy of reverent fear, not 'very bad'.
body: In older English 'awful' means inspiring awe (OED). The address echoes the invocation of Gray's 'Hymn to Adversity' and Horace's Ode to Fortune, both prayers to a dreaded power to be gentle. The final stanza moves 'To humbler functions': having seen Duty in the cosmos, the speaker commends himself to her guidance in ordinary life. The movement from cosmic to personal reverses the poem's earlier ascent and makes the closing prayer an act of humility.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'awful, adj.'
Thomas Gray, 'Hymn to Adversity' (1753), Thomas Gray Archive

title: 'made lowly wise'
short: Made wise through humility, echoing Raphael's advice to Adam in Paradise Lost: 'be lowly wise'.
body: In Paradise Lost VIII.173 Raphael tells Adam to restrain his curiosity about the heavens: 'be lowly wise'. Wordsworth's echo makes humility a form of wisdom and links his ode with Milton's argument for obedience. The speaker prays for 'The spirit of self-sacrifice' and 'The confidence of reason', a balanced pairing of feeling and judgment. The tone is that of a collect or private prayer, and the stanza moves away from the self-analysis of the middle stanzas toward simple petition.

sources.cite: Milton, Paradise Lost VIII.172-174 (Dartmouth Milton Reading Room)
William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3 (1896), Fenwick note, variants and notes to the poem

title: 'thy Bondman'
short: The speaker asks to live as Duty's servant, recalling the Christian paradox that God's service is 'perfect freedom'.
body: A bondman is a slave or serf. The paradox of free bondage is Pauline: 'Being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness' (Romans 6:18), and the Book of Common Prayer's Collect for Peace addresses God, 'whose service is perfect freedom'. The ode thus ends by resolving its opening contrast between freedom and law: true freedom is found in chosen obedience, the 'second Will more wise' of the suppressed stanza.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Romans 6:18
Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning Prayer, Second Collect, for Peace
